newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan petrol imports seen growing at snail's pace.
newsitem.headline: Japan petrol imports seen growing at snail's pace.

text.p: Flat retail prices and a weak yen are expected to stifle growth in Japan's gasoline imports this year, oil industry sources said on Tuesday.
The oil product import market, previously dominated by refiners, was liberalised a year ago allowing non-refiners to import products such as gasoline and kerosene for the first time in ten years.

However, only a handful of companies have taken advantage of the deregulation so far, mainly because profitability has deteriorated considerably compared with when the reform was officially decided in 1994.

"Imports by non-refiners are not expected to grow substantially this year with domestic retail prices and the yen expected to remain weak," said Akira Takahashi, managing director of the Oil Information Service Centre.

Gasoline imports by non-refiners in the last fiscal year which ended on March 31 totalled an estimated 100,000 kilolitres (kl), a trickle compared with Japan's annual demand of 50 million kl, Takahashi said.
"Imports will probably be only slightly above 100,000 kl this year," he said.
Profitability has diminished because in the run up to deregulation a price war broke out amongst gasoline stations, fearing an influx of cheap imports.
To combat imports, Japan's refiners also introduced a new wholesale pricing system which brought the price of gasoline down to levels competitive with imports.
The average national gasoline retail price was 106 yen per litre according to the latest statistics from the Oil Information Service Centre, down from 118 yen in April 1994.
Tax accounts for about half of the retail price.
Takashi Kawai, analyst with private Nikko Research Center said imports would become an attractive business only with a foreign exchange rate of around 90 to 100 yen to the dollar.
"If the yen rises against the dollar, imports could grow," Kawai said. "Firms will not take part in businesses which are not profitable," he said.
On Tuesday the dollar stood at around 126 yen, compared with levels of around 104 yen a year earlier.
An agricultural body, Zenno, which has a term contract with South Korea's Yukong Ltd to import 5,500 kl of gasoline per month said it was not planning to increase volume.
"The weaker yen against the dollar has made imports less profitable," an official with Zenno or the National Federation of Agricultural Cooperative Associations, said.

Zenno owns a chain of gasoline stations and has facilities needed for distribution, but the lack of facilities such as oil storage tanks make imports a tedious task for non-refiners, oil industry sources said.
Imports of kerosene fared better, with non-refiner imports reaching an estimated 400,000 kl, against annual demand of about 30 million kl.
The Oil Information Centre's Takahashi said kerosene imports from China were high.
"Kerosene made from the low-sulphur crude produced in China matches Japan's quality standards," Takahashi said.
However Takahashi said it was unclear whether kerosene imports by non-refiners would continue to grow. "Japanese demand depends on how cold the winter is," he said.
